e: Interior Gateway Protocols route within a single organisation's Autonomous System; Exterior Gateway Protocols route between organisations over the Internet
d: BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) is the only EGP in use today.

e: Each router tells its directly connected neighbours all the networks it knows, along with its own distance to each
d: Sometimes called "routing by rumour" — a router has no topology information beyond what its neighbours have advertised.

e: Each router describes itself and its directly connected interfaces/neighbours; this information is flooded unchanged to every router in the area
d: Every router ends up with the full topology and independently calculates the best routes from it.

e: Routing Information Protocol
d: Distance vector IGP. Uses hop count as its metric, max 15 hops. RIPv2 supports VLSM; RIPv1 does not. Rarely used outside very small or lab networks.

e: Interior Gateway Routing Protocol
d: Cisco-proprietary, distance vector IGP (now obsolete). Calculates a composite metric from bandwidth and optionally delay, load, reliability and MTU. Superseded by EIGRP; doesn't support VLSM.

e: Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol
d: Originally Cisco-proprietary but now published. Advanced distance vector IGP, calculating a composite metric similarly to IGRP.

e: Open Shortest Path First
d: Link state IGP. Refers to OSPFv2 unless stated otherwise. Uses cost as its metric, automatically derived from interface bandwidth by default.

e: Intermediate System to Intermediate System
d: Link state IGP, used mainly in Service Provider networks. Its metric acts like hop count unless manually configured — it doesn't automatically factor in bandwidth.

e: 1) Manually via router-id a.b.c.d 2) Highest IP of a loopback interface 3) Highest IP of a regular interface
d: Whichever rule matches first applies.

e: Routers send Hello packets to multicast 224.0.0.5, containing their own RID and a list of RIDs already seen
d: After the initial Hello both routers are in Init state; once they've both seen each other's RID, they become 2-way neighbours.

e: Full (fully adjacent) neighbours have exchanged Database Description packets (DBD) then any LSAs one has that the other doesn't, via Link-State Updates (LSUs)
d: Not all 2-way neighbours become full neighbours — see DR/BDR.

e: Routers exchange Hellos continually at set intervals; if no Hello arrives within the Dead interval (a multiple of Hello) the neighbour is considered dead
d: The router(s) that noticed the failure flood LSAs reflecting the change so others update their LSDBs and recalculate routes.

e: Routers reflood each LSA every 30 minutes by default, regardless of link changes
d: The refresh timer is separate per LSA, avoiding a network-wide surge from reflooding everything simultaneously.

e: On a broadcast segment (e.g. Ethernet) with multiple routers, one is elected Designated Router and another Backup Designated Router; the rest become DROther
d: All routers become full neighbours with the DR and BDR (which act as hubs of information) but not with each other, reducing LSA traffic. DR/BDR are elected per broadcast network, not per router, and aren't used on point-to-point links.

e: Highest OSPF interface priority wins DR, second-highest becomes BDR; highest RID breaks ties
d: Once elected there's no pre-emption — a new router joining, or a priority change, won't trigger a fresh election while the current DR/BDR are still up.

e: Down → Init → 2-Way → Exstart → Exchange → Loading → Full
OSPFv2 supports IPv4 only; OSPFv3 supports both IPv4 and IPv6
d: OSPFv2 is commonly used in IPv4-only networks; OSPFv3 is required for IPv6.

e: A single flat area means every router holds the full topology, which can exhaust router memory and forces a full reconvergence on any change
d: OSPF instead segments large networks into areas — a rule of thumb is up to 50 routers per area.

e: Area 0 (backbone/transit area) carries all inter-area traffic by default; regular (nonbackbone) areas connect end users to the backbone
d: Small networks don't need this and can run everything in Area 0.

e: An OSPF router with all of its interfaces in Area 0
A router with interfaces in multiple areas
d: Separates LSA flooding zones, is the primary point for (manually configured) area address summarisation, commonly sources default routes into its areas, and maintains a separate LSDB per connected area. Ideally connects to just two areas — the backbone plus one other — with three as the practical upper limit.

e: A router with all of its OSPF interfaces in one, non-backbone area
d: Learns inter-area routes to other areas from its ABR.

e: A router that redistributes routes from another routing protocol or static routes into OSPF
d: Routes redistributed into OSPF this way appear as External Routes.

e: (config-router)# network ip-address wildcard-mask area area-id
d: Enables OSPF on any interface whose IP falls within the given range, and advertises that interface's configured network and mask.

e: The inverse of a subnet mask — subtract each octet from 255
d: A 255.255.0.0 subnet mask becomes wildcard 0.0.255.255; a 255.255.255.252 mask becomes wildcard 0.0.0.3.

e: Advertises the connected subnet but sends no OSPF messages on that interface
d: Useful when there's no other router on the segment, or when there's a foreign-organisation OSPF router present that shouldn't see your internal topology. passive-interface default makes all interfaces passive by default; no passive-interface ifname re-activates specific ones.

e: Injects the router's own static default route into OSPF, making it an ASBR
d: The "always" keyword advertises the default route regardless of whether it's actually working.

e: Cost = Reference Bandwidth ÷ Interface Bandwidth
d: Default reference bandwidth is 100 Mbps, so both FastEthernet (100 Mbps) and GigabitEthernet (1000 Mbps) round up to a cost of 1 — meaning OSPF treats all links ≥100 Mbps as equal unless the reference bandwidth is manually raised.

e: ip ospf cost n directly sets a cost (recommended, doesn't affect anything else) · bandwidth speed sets a notional interface speed in Kbits, which is used to calculate cost
maximum-paths n balances load across up to n equal-cost, equal-Administrative-Distance paths
d: OSPF cannot do unequal-cost load balancing — EIGRP would be needed for that.

e: DR/BDR elections yes, manual neighbours no, Hello/Dead 10/40 seconds
d: Default for Ethernet and FDDI.

e: DR/BDR elections no, manual neighbours no, Hello/Dead 10/40 seconds
d: Default for PPP and HDLC links.

e: DR/BDR elections yes, manual neighbours required, Hello/Dead 30/120 seconds
d: Default for X.25 and Frame Relay; requires a neighbor command since it can't multicast Hellos.

e: (config-router)# neighbor address
d: Required whenever an OSPF network type doesn't support automatic neighbour discovery (non-broadcast types).

e: Interfaces up/up, in the same subnet, in the same area, matching Hello/Dead timers, unique RIDs, and (if used) matching authentication
d: If unmet, routers won't even show as neighbours.

t: OSPF neighbour relationship — MTU and network type
e: Matching MTU and matching OSPF network type are also required
d: Unlike the other requirements, a mismatch here still lets routers see each other as neighbours — but LSAs won't actually be exchanged, so OSPF silently fails to work.

e: (config-router) shutdown
d: Retains configuration but stops all OSPF activity: clears the LSDB, drops neighbour relationships, and removes OSPF-learned routes from the routing table.
